data.title: Proximity Proteomics Revealed Dicer1 and Transporters as Client Proteins of Aha1
data.projectDescription: Co-chaperone Aha1 activates HSP90 ATPase to promote the folding of client proteins. However, the client proteins of Aha1 are largely unknown. By employing ascorbate peroxidase (APEX) based proximity labeling, we identified 32 proximity proteins of HSP90 that are modulated by genetic depletion of Aha1. Among them, Dicer1 is one of the top-ranked proteins, which were further confirmed by streptavidin pull-down followed by Western blot analysis, demonstrating the reliability of the approach. Flag pull-down result showed interactions between endogenous HSP90 and Dicer1 and Aha1. The Dicer1 level is regulated synergistically by Aha1 and HSP90. Maturation-dependent interaction results showed a preferential binding of Aha1 and HSP90 to nascently translated Dicer1. Reconstitution of Aha1-depleted cells with WT Aha1 restored Dicer1 level, while the HSP90-binding-defective E67K mutant exhibited partial restoration. Moreover, knockdown of Aha1 and inhibition of HSP90 can diminish the levels of mature miRNA, let-7b and mir-30a. Overall, our study uncovers, for the first time, Dicer1 and transporter proteins as clients of Aha1 and HSP90.
data.sampleProcessingProtocol: Proximity labeling was conducted as described previously. In brief, approximately 20 million cells were incubated in complete medium containing 500 µM of biotin phenol for 30 min followed by incubation with 1.0 mM H2O2 for 1 min. The reaction was quenched by washing the cells with a quenching buffer (5 mM of Trolox, 10 mM of sodium ascorbate and 10 mM of sodium azide in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and PBS twice each. Cells were lysed with 500 µL of CelLytic M (Sigma) containing 1% protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma) and the above-described quenching buffer. The cell lysates were centrifuged at 13,000 RPM at 4°C for 10 min to remove cell debris. Approximately 1 mg of total proteins were incubated with streptavidin-conjugated agarose beads (Pierce Thermo) overnight at 4°C. The beads were subsequently washed with 500 µL of CelLytic M twice, 1 M KCl, 0.1 M Na2CO3, and twice with CelLytic M again. Biotinalyted proteins were eluted by incubating the beads in 3× protein loading buffer containing 2 mM biotin at 95°C for 5 min. The resulting proteins were resolved by a 15% SDS-PAGE gel for approximately 1 cm. Gel bands corresponding to protein molecular weight larger than 15 kDa were excised and cut into 1 mm3 cubes for in-gel trypsin digestion. Cysteine reduction and alkylation were conducted by incubating the gel pieces in 10 mM dithiothreitol and 55 mM iodoacetamide for 1 h at 37°C and 20 min at RT in dark, respectively. The proteins were subsequently digested with 200 ng of modified MS-grade trypsin (Pierce) in 50 mM NH4HCO3 at 37°C overnight. The peptide mixture was dried in a Speed-vac and desalted with OMIX C18 pipette tips (Agilent Technologies).
data.dataProcessingProtocol: Raw files were processed using MaxQuant (version 2.0.1.0). Methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation were specified as variable modifications; and cysteine carbamidomethylation as a fixed modification. Mass tolerance for both MS1 and MS2 were set to 20 ppm. A maximum of two missed trypsin cleavage was allowed, and the peptides were filtered at 1% false discovery rate (FDR). Match between runs option was enabled with a match time window of 0.7 min. For protein identification, peptide spectra were searched against a target-decoy human Uniprot database proteome (UP000005640) and filtered at 1% protein FDR. Normalized label-free quantification with a minimum ratio count of 2 was used for protein quantification.
